subject: economics
title: Demand changes for complementary products — Arden
stem:
All places and data are constructed. In Arden, a new commuter rail line opens. Bicycle parking at its stations is free, while the price of bicycles is unchanged.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Bicycle assemblers have considerable spare capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define demand.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why bicycle demand may rise.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using a demand and supply diagram, explain the likely equilibrium effect, assuming upward-sloping supply.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: The quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices.
Over a specified period, other relevant conditions held constant.
Bicycles and rail travel may be complements for combined journeys.
Cheaper/more convenient rail access can increase desired bicycle purchases at each bicycle price.
Correct price/quantity axes, D1, D2 and S.
D shifts right; new equilibrium has higher price and quantity.
At the original bicycle price, excess demand develops.
Price rises and quantity supplied extends until demand equals supply; this is not a movement along unchanged demand.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
Supply can respond more readily, limiting price pressure relative to a capacity-constrained case. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

subtopic: Signals when a market is in shortage
stem:
All places and data are constructed. In Caldin, a shop posts a price below the competitive equilibrium for refill bottles, without a legal price control.

Answer parts (a)–(c) using the initial scenario. For part (d) only, consider the following additional evidence, which may change an initial assumption.

Additional application evidence: Sellers can quickly order additional bottles.

parts.prompt: Distinguish equilibrium from shortage.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the incentive for the posted price to rise.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain how price performs both a rationing and an incentive function.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how the additional evidence changes or qualifies the economic interpretation in this case.

steps.text: Equilibrium is a price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
A shortage is excess quantity demanded at a particular price.
Buyers compete for the limited supply and unsatisfied demand remains.
Sellers can raise price while still selling their output.
Higher price reduces quantity demanded among some buyers.
This rations the scarce bottles by willingness and ability to pay.
Higher price raises potential producer returns.
Firms expand quantity supplied or direct resources toward bottles; access need not be equitable.
Identify the economic determinant, constraint or model assumption affected by this evidence, distinguishing it from the conditions used in the initial analysis.
A responsive supply expansion helps reduce the shortage as prices adjust. A justified causal link is required for this explanation mark.

title: PED and a revenue decision — Doreva
stem: All places and data are constructed. In Doreva, a controlled pricing study reduces a product's price from 10 to 9 crowns. Quantity demanded rises from 200 to 230 units per week.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate PED using initial-value percentages.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in total revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one reason why the result may not hold in another month.

steps.text: Price falls 10%; quantity demanded rises 15%.
PED = −1.50; absolute magnitude 1.50, so demand is elastic.
Initial revenue = 10 × 200 = 2000 crowns.
New revenue = 0.90 ×1.15 × initial revenue = 2070 crowns.
Revenue rises by 3.50%.
The number/closeness of substitutes, consumer income or tastes may change.
The estimate is conditional on the study period; a different demand curve or elasticity can change the revenue effect.

subject: economics
title: Income elasticity and inferior goods — Elarin
stem: All places and data are constructed. In Elarin, household income rises by 5%, while demand for a low-cost cereal falls by 10%, with its price and other influences unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define income elasticity of demand.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate YED and classify the cereal.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a negative YED does not imply an upward-sloping demand curve.

steps.text: Responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in income.
YED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in income.
YED = −2.
A negative YED classifies the cereal as an inferior good over this income range.
YED changes income; the law of demand changes the good's own price.
A rise in income shifts demand for this inferior good left.

All places, observations and values below are constructed for practice. Case Doreva: A storm destroys part of the fruit harvest; unchilled fruit spoils quickly. Growers can add trees only over several seasons. The council considers shared cold storage, while rural households rely heavily on farm income.

A separate controlled demand study holds all non-price influences constant. It is not a before/after estimate of the policies in the text.

stem:
All places, observations and values below are constructed for practice. Case Gavela: Private car journeys create local air pollution and delays for other road users. The city plans a bus fare subsidy; buses have spare seats outside the peak but are full during rush hour. Low-income shift workers travel when service is infrequent.

A separate controlled demand study holds all non-price influences constant. It is not a before/after estimate of the policies in the text.

| Study observation | Price (crowns/unit) | Quantity demanded (units/week) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial | 20 | 100 |
| New | 25 | 90 |

Show numerical working. Give exact values or round to two decimal places, and retain relevant units.

A further case detail: The public budget is tight and service providers cannot expand capacity immediately.

parts.prompt:

steps.text: A cost imposed on third parties by consumption.

Shift effective supply down/right; consumer fare falls and journeys rise.
The subsidy lowers the price needed to cover each bus journey.
The size of the expansion depends on available capacity and demand responsiveness.

A lower bus fare lowers the relative cost of bus travel.
Some consumers switch, shifting demand for car journeys left.
The effect may be small where bus frequency, routes or travel time are unsuitable.
Peak buses are already full.

title: Clean-water monitoring — Pavira
stem:
All places, observations and values below are constructed for practice. Case Pavira: A public water-quality alert is broadcast to every household in range. Private water filters are sold separately. Some upstream firms pollute, and poorer residents cannot easily buy filters. The authority considers public monitoring and enforceable discharge standards.

A separate controlled demand study holds all non-price influences constant. It is not a before/after estimate of the policies in the text.

| Study observation | Price (crowns/unit) | Quantity demanded (units/week) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial | 20 | 100 |
| New | 25 | 90 |

Firms omit damage to water users from private costs.
Reducing excess polluting output or emissions can recover welfare.
Label filter price/quantity and D1/D2.
Shift D right.
A normal good's demand rises with income at each price.
It is a shift due to income rather than a movement due to filter price.
The authority needs reliable information about emissions.

Monitoring and penalties must make compliance credible.

title: Tax incidence and a packaging policy — Ilyra
subtopic: Tax incidence and a packaging policy
stem:
This is a fictional policy case in Ilyra. Inverse demand is P=100−Q and inverse private supply is P=20+Q; P is crowns per unit and Q is units per day. Curves are linear over the range used. The government considers a specific tax of 12 crowns per unit on disposable packages. Demand is relatively unresponsive for small food vendors; refill substitutes require an initial equipment purchase.

This complete Paper 3 style case awards 20 marks for part (a) and 10 for the policy recommendation. Show working; give exact answers or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the untaxed equilibrium price and quantity.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the taxed quantity, consumer price and producer net price.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate daily government tax revenue and explain why revenue is not itself a net welfare gain.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the daily loss of total surplus if there are no externalities and explain why tax revenue is excluded from that loss.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain how a tax can still improve welfare when packaging has external costs.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a policy or policy package to reduce disposable packaging while considering the constraints faced by small vendors.

steps.text: Q=40 units/day.
P=60 crowns/unit.
Q=34 units/day.
Consumer price=66 crowns/unit.
Producer net price=54 crowns/unit.
408 crowns/day.
Tax revenue transfers purchasing power to government; it is not newly created resources, so other stakeholder effects must also be counted.
36 crowns/day.
It is the triangle of mutually beneficial trades prevented; tax revenue is a transfer, not itself a social loss.
Unpriced disposal damage creates a gap between MSC and MPC.
The private equilibrium can then involve excessive packaging.
A tax raises the private marginal cost faced by decision makers.
It can reduce output toward MSB=MSC.
A correctly sized tax reflects marginal external damage at the efficient output.
The no-externality loss in part (iv) is therefore not automatically the net welfare effect in the actual case.

A phased tax with recycling/refill support can alter incentives while helping vendors finance substitutes. Weigh monitoring, regressivity and uncertain external costs; an alternative combination of deposit-return and standards is acceptable if its mechanism and suitability are justified.
Variant-specific recommendation: Compare a monitored pilot with immediate broad rollout, using the quantitative evidence and acknowledging the cost of delay.

stem:
This is a fictional policy case in Lunara. Inverse demand is P=100−Q and inverse private supply is P=20+Q; P is crowns per unit and Q is units per day. Curves are linear over the range used. title: Pollution damage and efficient output — Orlen
stem:
This is a fictional policy case in Orlen. Inverse demand is P=100−Q and inverse private supply is P=20+Q; P is crowns per unit and Q is units per day. Curves are linear over the range used. Production creates constant marginal external damage of 12 crowns per unit. MSB equals private demand; MSC equals private supply plus that damage. Monitoring output is easy, but actual emissions differ across firms.

This complete Paper 3 style case awards 20 marks for part (a) and 10 for the policy recommendation. Show working; give exact answers or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate private market output and price.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the socially efficient output and associated MSB.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the daily welfare loss of the unregulated market and explain why the stated external-cost wedge is used.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate revenue from a tax equal to marginal external damage.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain why an emissions charge may be preferable to an output tax for heterogeneous firms.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a policy to address pollution, drawing on the efficient-output calculation and the monitoring constraints.

steps.text: Qm=40 units/day.
P=60 crowns/unit.
Q*=34 units/day.
66 crowns/unit.
36 crowns/day.
At Qm, MSC−MSB equals the external-cost wedge; the gap narrows linearly to zero at Q*.
Tax=12 crowns/unit and taxed output=34 units/day.
Revenue=12×34.
408 crowns/day.
An output tax treats units alike even when emissions per unit differ.
It may not reward cleaner technology sufficiently.
An emissions charge attaches a cost to measured damage-generating activity.
Firms can respond by reducing emissions intensity as well as output.
Accurate emissions measurement is required.
Higher monitoring cost or weak enforcement may favour a simpler policy in this context.

Indicative model reasoning (not an additive checklist): A corrective output tax matches the given constant damage model and reduces output toward Q*. Yet varying emissions intensities strengthen the case for a monitored emissions charge or standards. Weigh enforcement cost, cleaner technology incentives and distribution, using the calculated welfare loss as a model estimate rather than an observed empirical gain.
Variant-specific recommendation: Compare a monitored pilot with immediate broad rollout, using the quantitative evidence and acknowledging the cost of delay.

subject: economics
title: Pollution damage and efficient output — Quorin
stem:
This is a fictional policy case in Quorin. Inverse demand is P=120−Q and inverse private supply is P=24+Q; P is crowns per unit and Q is units per day. Curves are linear over the range used. Production creates constant marginal external damage of 20 crowns per unit. MSB equals private demand; MSC equals private supply plus that damage. Monitoring output is easy, but actual emissions differ across firms.

This complete Paper 3 style case awards 20 marks for part (a) and 10 for the policy recommendation. Show working; give exact answers or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Benefits arrive with a lag, while some affected households need immediate assistance.

parts.prompt: Calculate private market output and price.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the socially efficient output and associated MSB.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the daily welfare loss of the unregulated market and explain why the stated external-cost wedge is used.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate revenue from a tax equal to marginal external damage.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain why an emissions charge may be preferable to an output tax for heterogeneous firms.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend a policy to address pollution, drawing on the efficient-output calculation and the monitoring constraints.

This is a fictional policy case in Vesper. Inverse demand is P=110−Q and inverse private supply is P=22+Q; P is crowns per unit and Q is units per day. Curves are linear over the range used. A legal maximum price is set at 58 crowns. The good is a staple. The authority cannot guarantee every household receives a ration; some retailers cut opening hours.

This complete Paper 3 style case awards 20 marks for part (a) and 10 for the policy recommendation. Show working; give exact answers or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: The authority has weak enforcement capacity and limited reliable household records.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the unrestricted equilibrium.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate quantities supplied and demanded at the ceiling.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the shortage and legal market sales revenue, assuming all supplied units sell.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the government cost of buying the shortage abroad at the ceiling price, if this were feasible.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain why a lower legal price need not improve access for every poor household.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend an approach to improve staple access for low-income households, using the shortage and cost evidence.

title: Plant scale, unit costs and competition — Xandor
subtopic: Plant scale, unit costs and competition
stem:
This fictional case concerns a recycling processor in Xandor. At its current plant scale, daily output is 100 units and total daily cost is 1500 crowns. A larger plant could produce 200 units at a total daily cost of 2600 crowns. The selling price is assumed constant at 20 crowns/unit in this project comparison, and all output can be sold. These are alternative fully adjusted plant scales, not a short-run variable-labour experiment. Larger processing capacity could lower collection charges, but an exclusive collection contract may prevent rival entry.

This complete Paper 3 style case awards 20 marks for part (a) and 10 for the policy recommendation. Show working; give exact answers or round to two decimal places.

Implementation evidence: Implementation can be phased and audited before nationwide expansion.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate current average total cost and profit.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate average total cost and profit at the larger plant.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in average cost and the change in daily sales revenue.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the additional cost per extra unit between the plant choices and explain its interpretation.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Explain why these data can indicate economies of scale without contradicting diminishing marginal returns.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Recommend an approach to recycling-processing expansion that considers unit costs, access and competition.
